articles.title: Accessibility
articles.summary: Designing products, services and environments for equitable access, addressing barriers for people with disabilities and a wider range of access needs.

text.content: Overview

rich_text.plain_text: Overview

text.content: Accessibility is about equitable access to products, services and environments. It considers the different ways people perceive information, understand it and interact with the world, and the barriers that can prevent them from participating.

rich_text.plain_text: Accessibility is about equitable access to products, services and environments. It considers the different ways people perceive information, understand it and interact with the world, and the barriers that can prevent them from participating.

text.content: In digital products, barriers can emerge in places that designers and developers may commonly overlook, or haven't adequately considered. For example; a form that can't be completed using a keyboard, text that becomes unreadable when enlarged, or an error message that relies entirely on colour.

rich_text.plain_text: In digital products, barriers can emerge in places that designers and developers may commonly overlook, or haven't adequately considered. For example; a form that can't be completed using a keyboard, text that becomes unreadable when enlarged, or an error message that relies entirely on colour.

text.content: Disability is central to accessibility, encompassing physical, sensory, cognitive and other experiences. Access needs can also be shaped by neurodivergence, including ADHD and dyslexia, ageing, temporary injuries and situational limitations. People's needs differ, and can change depending on their environment, the technology they're using and what they're trying to do.

Access needs can also be shaped by neurodivergence, including ADHD and dyslexia, ageing, temporary injuries and situational limitations. People's needs differ, and can change depending on their environment, the technology they're using and what they're trying to do.

text.content: The aim is to make products, services and environments accessible to as many people as possible by identifying and addressing barriers. Some are technical; others arise from design, language, content or assumptions about how people interact. Different access needs can require different approaches, and no single solution will work for everyone in every situation.

text.content: The problem with the 'default' user

rich_text.plain_text: The problem with the 'default' user

text.content: A lot of the technology we use is designed around assumptions about the people using it. That they can see a screen, hear audio, use a mouse, read and process information in a particular way, or complete a task within a certain amount of time.

rich_text.plain_text: A lot of the technology we use is designed around assumptions about the people using it. That they can see a screen, hear audio, use a mouse, read and process information in a particular way, or complete a task within a certain amount of time.

text.content: These assumptions often go unnoticed by the people making them. For someone who doesn't fit that imagined 'default' user, the consequences can be significant.

text.content: Consider how much of everyday life now depends on digital services. Banking, healthcare, education, employment and government services are increasingly accessed online. An inaccessible interface can prevent someone from completing an essential task, accessing information or participating independently.

text.content: Access needs change

rich_text.plain_text: Access needs change

text.content: Access needs can be permanent, temporary or situational. Someone recovering from an injury might be unable to use a mouse. A person in a noisy environment might rely on captions. Ageing can affect vision, hearing or dexterity. These experiences aren't interchangeable, but they show why designing for a narrow idea of ability leaves people out.

articles.title: Affect Heuristic
articles.summary: A mental shortcut where our feelings about something influence how we judge its risks, benefits and overall value.

text.content: Overview

rich_text.plain_text: Overview

text.content: The affect heuristic describes our tendency to use feelings as a shortcut when making judgements and decisions. A natural moment of human mental parkour.

rich_text.plain_text: The affect heuristic describes our tendency to use feelings as a shortcut when making judgements and decisions. A natural moment of human mental parkour.

text.content: Affect

rich_text.plain_text: Affect

text.content: refers to the positive or negative feelings we associate with something. A product might feel trustworthy, a new technology might seem threatening, or an idea might appeal to us before we've given it much thought.

rich_text.plain_text: refers to the positive or negative feelings we associate with something. A product might feel trustworthy, a new technology might seem threatening, or an idea might appeal to us before we've given it much thought.

text.content: Those feelings can influence how we assess something, particularly its risks and benefits. When we feel positively about something, we're usually more inclined to see the benefits and downplay the risks. When we feel negatively, the risks can seem greater and the benefits less convincing.

When we feel positively about something, we're usually more inclined to see the benefits and downplay the risks. When we feel negatively, the risks can seem greater and the benefits less convincing.

text.content: We make countless judgements every day, often with incomplete information and limited time to think things through. Feelings help us navigate that complexity, drawing on previous experiences and associations without requiring us to analyse every detail.

text.content: Confirmation bias describes the tendency to seek or interpret information in ways that support what we already believe or expect. It can also influence what we remember. articles.summary: Ethical design examines how design decisions affect people, whose interests they serve, and the responsibilities that come with those choices.

text.content: Overview

text.content: Every design decision has consequences. Some are obvious, such as whether a product is accessible or how much personal information it collects. Others are less visible: whose behaviour a system encourages, which interests it prioritises, and who bears the cost when something goes wrong.

Others are less visible: whose behaviour a system encourages, which interests it prioritises, and who bears the cost when something goes wrong.

text.content: Ethical design is the practice of examining these consequences and making deliberate, accountable choices about them. It draws on moral philosophy, human rights and professional ethics, with related approaches such as value-sensitive design examining how human values can be considered throughout the development of technology.

text.content: There's no single formula for determining whether a design is ethical. Different values can pull in different directions, and the questions extend beyond whether a product works as intended. Who decided what it should do? Who benefits? Who might be disadvantaged, excluded or harmed? And what happens when the interests of the people using a product conflict with those of the organisation providing it?

rich_text.plain_text: Ethical questions come up at every stage of design, from deciding which problems are worth solving to understanding what happens after a product is released.

text.content: This means questioning assumptions, weighing competing interests and looking beyond the people a product was originally designed for. It also means questioning what success looks like. A product optimised primarily for time spent, conversion or retention may reward behaviours that serve the organisation without necessarily benefiting its users. Those metrics aren't inherently unethical, but they don't exist in a vacuum. They're incomplete measures of success.

text.content: Professional standards can provide useful reference points. The ACM Code of Ethics identifies avoiding harm, respecting privacy, fairness and accessibility among the responsibilities of computing professionals.[1] Accessibility standards such as WCAG provide testable requirements that help translate broad commitments into practical design and development work.[2]

text.content: People rarely agree on every value or how competing values should be balanced. Privacy, safety, autonomy, accessibility, transparency and commercial sustainability can all matter, sometimes in conflicting ways.

text.content: Responsibility and accountability

rich_text.plain_text: Responsibility and accountability

text.content: Designers may recognise a harmful pattern without having the authority to change the business model, performance targets or organisational priorities behind it. Ethical design therefore depends on more than individual professional conduct. Leadership, governance, incentives and accountability all shape what teams can realistically do.

text.content: Responsibility also extends beyond release. Decisions made with reasonable intentions can produce unexpected harm, and responding to those consequences is part of ethical practice.

text.content: An ethical approach doesn't promise perfect outcomes. It asks that consequences are taken seriously, competing interests are examined, affected people are heard, and decisions can be explained and challenged.

articles.title: Inclusive Design
articles.summary: Inclusive design considers human diversity, challenges assumptions about who we're designing for, and involves people affected by design decisions in shaping them.

text.content: Overview

rich_text.plain_text: Overview

text.content: Inclusive design acknowledges that there is no single, representative user. It asks whose needs are being considered, whose experiences are missing and how those differences might change the decisions being made.

rich_text.plain_text: Inclusive design acknowledges that there is no single, representative user. It asks whose needs are being considered, whose experiences are missing and how those differences might change the decisions being made.

text.content: Designers make assumptions about the people they're designing for

rich_text.plain_text: Designers make assumptions about the people they're designing for

text.content: . Some are deliberate and informed by research and experience. Others are shaped by the perspectives of the people making decisions, and the circumstances they're familiar with.

text.content: Inclusion should be part of design from the beginning, not an optional consideration or something added at the end. Inclusive design is about preventing assumptions from becoming barriers. It considers differences in people's abilities, identities, experiences and circumstances, and involves people who might otherwise be overlooked or excluded.

Inclusive design is about preventing assumptions from becoming barriers. It considers differences in people's abilities, identities, experiences and circumstances, and involves people who might otherwise be overlooked or excluded.

text.content: People can encounter physical, cognitive, sensory, social, cultural or economic barriers, sometimes multiple intersecting at once. Their needs can also change with their circumstances. What works well for one person may be difficult or even impossible for another to use.

text.content: In practice

rich_text.plain_text: In practice

text.content: Inclusive design begins with understanding who might be excluded and why. This means looking beyond the people who are easiest to recruit, already use a product or rarely encounter barriers when using it.

rich_text.plain_text: Inclusive design begins with understanding who might be excluded and why. This means looking beyond the people who are easiest to recruit, already use a product or rarely encounter barriers when using it.

text.content: Research and participation help uncover assumptions a design team might never question on its own.[4] This is especially important when the people making design decisions have little experience of the barriers others face.

text.content: People affected by design decisions should have a meaningful say in shaping them. Their perspectives can challenge requirements, question familiar design patterns or reveal that a proposed solution doesn't address the problem. Co-design is one approach to creating a more equitable design process, where people help shape decisions and solutions rather than being consulted only to provide feedback.

text.content: Inclusive design also shapes how products and services are developed. Different ways to interact, support for assistive technologies, understandable language and flexibility across environments can reduce barriers. Just as in the design process, these implementation choices should be informed by the people who encounter those barriers.

text.content: Inclusion doesn't mean identical experiences

rich_text.plain_text: Inclusion doesn't mean identical experiences

text.content: People don't all need the same things, and sometimes those needs conflict. What makes something accessible or useful for one person might make it harder for someone else.

text.content: Flexibility, personalisation and alternative ways of completing a task can help, but they also raise questions about complexity, consistency and maintenance. Inclusive design means considering how those trade-offs affect different people.

text.content: Participation and influence

rich_text.plain_text: Participation and influence

text.content: Inviting people into a research session doesn't automatically make a design process inclusive. Sometimes participation amounts to little more than lip service: people are consulted, their feedback is documented, and the organisation carries on doing what it intended to do anyway.

text.content: Meaningful involvement requires attention to who participates, how they're supported and what influence they have. It doesn't mean every suggestion must be adopted, but people should have a genuine opportunity to shape decisions, and organisations should be able to explain how their input was considered. No individual can represent an entire community.

text.content: Inclusive design overlaps with accessibility, universal design and co-design. Their boundaries aren't always clear, and different organisations describe them differently.

text.content: Accessibility concerns whether people, particularly disabled people, can access and use a product, service or environment. Inclusive design is one approach to identifying and preventing the barriers that affect accessibility.[1]

text.content: Universal design, which has roots in architecture and product design, aims to make products and environments usable by as many people as possible without specialised adaptation.[2] Inclusive design approaches often place greater emphasis on individual differences, flexible solutions and the participation of people who might otherwise be excluded.[3]
